extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative government, and democratic theory
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of religion's role in democracy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting the principles by which religion influences the stability and character of democratic (particularly American) institutions, as argued in a classic political-philosophical text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of Church and State
rubrics_metrics.description: Care taken by the Americans to separate the Church from the State—The laws, public opinion, and even the exertions of the clergy concur to promote this end—Influence of religion upon the mind in the United States attributable to this cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites legal and constitutional provisions excluding clergy from civil office (e.g., constitutions of New York, North Carolina, Virginia, etc.) and emphasizes that public opinion and clergy behavior (withdrawing from power) jointly produce a durable religious influence. The passage treats separation as a causal explanation for religion's strong but non-political authority in America.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy abstention from political office and parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the American clergy 'filled no public appointments... are not even represented in the legislative assemblies' and 'eschewed all parties', making abstention a professional pride.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that when clergy deliberately avoid civil/military office and party entanglements, their moral authority is preserved; the exception noted is educational roles. Examples and state constitutional clauses are cited as institutionalizing this abstention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion must avoid alliance with political power
rubrics_metrics.description: When a religion contracts an alliance with a government it 'commits the same error...it risks that authority which is rightfully its own'—alliances make religion fragile and partisan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains the trade-off: state alliance can give religion temporal power but sacrifices its universality and long-term durability. Mixed alignment drags religion into transient political passions and may force it to defend political allies rather than spiritual principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion regulates manners and domestic life, thereby stabilizing the State
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion 'directs the manners of the community, and by regulating domestic life it regulates the State.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: high respect for the marriage tie, women's moral influence, and domestic order produce citizens accustomed to moderation and obedience to law. The passage links private moral habits to public political stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion provides moral restraints that check innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion 'confines the imagination of the Americans within certain limits, and checks the passion of innovation' so that 'before it can perpetrate innovation, certain primal and immutable principles are laid down.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument is that religion imposes barriers and scruples that curb radical or rash political experimentation; this restraint makes innovations more circumspect and institutions more durable. The text frames this as a positive check on disruptive tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion is indispensable to maintaining republican institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Americans regard religious belief as 'indispensable to the maintenance of republican institutions'—'Despotism may govern without faith, but liberty cannot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book claims that as political ties loosen in republics, a moral tie supplied by religion becomes more necessary; religion thus supplies the civic virtue and restraint required for self-government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Christian morality across sects fosters social cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Although sects differ in worship, 'they all agree in respect to the duties which are due from man to man' and 'Christian morality is everywhere the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage argues that doctrinal differences matter little for social order so long as sects share the same basic moral code; society benefits when religious diversity is accompanied by moral agreement rather than doctrinal conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two great dangers to religion: schism and indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: The two great dangers which threaten the existence of religions are schism and indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schism may replace one faith with another rather than eliminate religiosity, while indifference (lukewarmness) causes believers to drift into scepticism without adopting a new belief. The text contrasts these threats and explains how indifference can be especially corrosive because it produces loss by attrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious strength depends on universal human sentiments rather than state support
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion that rests on universal sentiments (the consolations of affliction, desire of a future life) can defy time; religion tied to worldly interests becomes as fragile as temporal powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author claims that religions grounded in universally shared human feelings endure, whereas those allied to particular political interests or temporal authorities become vulnerable to the fate of those powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad elementary instruction and practical experience support democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The instruction of the American people: elementary notions, doctrine and evidences of religion, history of country, and leading constitutional features are widespread; 'practical experience more serviceable to the Americans than book-learning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New England is cited as teaching citizens religion, national history, and constitutional knowledge; even in less literate regions opinion diffusion is rapid. The text emphasizes general civic education and practical habit over elite literary or theoretical learning as sustaining democratic institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion favors religion when unbelief is concealed and belief displayed
rubrics_metrics.description: Because 'those who do not believe, conceal their incredulity; and... those who believe, display their faith, public opinion pronounces itself in favor of religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This social dynamic—public display by believers and private concealment by unbelievers—helps maintain outward religious norms and social honor for religion. Illustrative anecdote: a New York court rejecting a witness who declared disbelief in God as destroying confidence in his testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious zeal linked with patriotism to extend and secure republican institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans form societies to send ministers and found schools and churches in new Western States 'lest religion should be suffered to die away... and the rising States be less fitted to enjoy free institutions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missionary activity and religious settlement on the frontier are described as deliberate political acts to preserve republicanism; missionaries are often also political actors who value both religion and worldly goods and see the survival of other republics as tied to their religious character.
